source.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
source.authors: Qingyu Yin; Chak Tou Leong; Lin-Yi Yang; Wenxuan Huang; Wenjie Li; Xi-Ting Wang; Jaehong Yoon; Yun Xing; Yun Xing; Jin-Jin Gu

page_placements.theme: Reasoning models: the refusal signal depends on chain-of-thought position, and reasoning can carry, reverse or gate it

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full preprint; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study probes refusal signals across reasoning positions and intervenes on attention heads, then measures refusal-related outcomes in reasoning models. This is a conceptual test of refusal mediation in reasoning models, but it does not apply the original difference-in-means direction intervention.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal-score trajectories and attention-head ablations in reasoning models. The prober's validation accuracy is a predictive check, not a causal test of the claimed direction. The initial safety benchmark and the fine-tuning/data-selection results are not included as rows: they do not intervene on or measure the claimed direction, and the fine-tuning deliberately induces refusal. The study does not test harmfulness judgment separately from refusal.
record.test_reason: The study uses a logistic-regression refusal probe on last-layer hidden states as a tool, justified by Arditi et al.'s linear refusal direction. It never builds a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, and never ablates or adds a direction to test mediation. Its causal interventions target attention heads, not a direction. Its measures are probe scores, ASR after head ablation, and ASR after fine-tuning. So it does not test V1 or V8. Its own findings (refusal cliff, suppression heads) fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Poorly aligned reasoning models keep refusal intention during thinking, but it drops at the final tokens (the refusal cliff). Sparse Refusal Suppression Heads drive this drop, and ablating them restores refusal. Fine-tuning on the 700 examples with the largest cliff (1.7% of the data) gives safety comparable to full-data training, with little reasoning-benchmark cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a linear refusal prober, traces and ablates attention heads, and uses a refusal-cliff score for data selection. It does not construct a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction or project that direction out or add it.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal signal varies by model alignment, token position, layer depth, and whether thinking is truncated; ablation outcomes also vary with selected-head fraction and prompt benchmark.

fits_no_version.finding: In poorly aligned reasoning models, a linear refusal probe's score plateaus during thinking and then drops sharply at the thinking-end template tokens. The drop is strongest in deep layers. Well-aligned models show no such drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-predictive linear signals in reasoning models are present during reasoning but suppressed at the final template tokens ('refusal cliff').

fits_no_version.finding: A sparse set of attention heads contributes negatively to the refusal probe logit. Ablating 3% of them reduces ASR below 10%; ablating 10% more than doubles the probe refusal score, compared against random-head controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal suppression in reasoning models is carried by a small set of attention heads whose ablation restores refusal.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says source code will be released upon publication but gives no URL.
record.problems: The study uses a learned refusal probe and treats its scores as refusal intention; the probe is trained using refusal responses and harmless compliant responses. The supplied results do not directly establish that the probe direction mediates refusal. Ablation results are mostly shown in figures, with no uncertainty estimates reported, and the claimed capability preservation is evaluated for fine-tuning rather than head ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 baseline safety benchmark rates and Table 2 fine-tuning/data-selection results were not extracted because they do not test the claimed direction or its removal/addition. Prober validation accuracy was omitted because it measures prediction accuracy, not causal mediation. Figure 5 and Figure 8 results are included only at the reported model or aggregate level; no unreported numeric values were inferred.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction; no ablation or addition of a direction; no capability check after a direction intervention.

Whether a single difference-in-means direction mediates refusal in reasoning models (ablation removes, addition induces) is not tested. Only a learned linear probe is read out, and only heads are intervened on.

record.verdict_notes: The probe is trained on refusal responses to AdvBench prompts versus compliant responses to harmless UltraChat prompts. It therefore mixes harmfulness and refusal, and it is a learned logistic regression, not a mean-difference vector. Head-ablation results appear per model only in Figure 8. No uncertainty is reported, and no capability check is run after head ablation.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction is identified and projected out or added across layers and positions; general capability after such an intervention is not assessed.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is performed.
No attack is tested as suppressing the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.
The study does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
The study does not measure harmfulness judgment independently from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the claimed direction is reported.
Safety fine-tuning is used as a mitigation, but the study does not test how training determines whether the claimed removable direction exists.
The study tests refusal signals and head interventions in reasoning models, but not the original difference-in-means direction or its addition/removal.

relation.reason: Says the refusal direction can be found with a linear classifier and uses the probe throughout. Never tests whether a direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: Uses a logistic-regression refusal probe (last layer, final token), citing Arditi et al. for linearity, as a tool. No difference-in-means direction is built, and no direction is ablated or added. Interventions are on attention heads. The probe-score cliff is a related construct, so it does not test V1/V8.

source_check.notes: Internal inconsistencies: the intro says top 1.3% of data and ASR below 5%; the abstract says 1.7%; Table 2 has 700 of 40k (98.3% reduction) with Cliff-as-a-judge ASR 3.0-6.0%. Section 4.2 says Figure 6 shows ablation results, but they are in Figure 8. Appendix B names R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as the SFT base, yet Table 2 also reports R1-8B. No verdicts on the record, and none are owed.

statements.correction: Section 3: score rises, plateaus, then drops at thinking-end template tokens. Section 4.2: ablating the top-3% Refusal Suppression Heads cuts harmful-output rate below 10% (R1-7B, OR1-7B, R1-8B, R1-14B; JailbreakBench and WildJailbreak; per-model values figure-only).
statements.problem: The content is right. The ASR-below-10% claim comes from Section 4.2 / Figure 8, which neither cited row (r1, r12) records. 3% means the top 3% of heads by negative contribution, a selection threshold.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The reasoning models and conditions examined in this study
reader_labels.reason: Refusal scores show a terminal-position cliff in poorly aligned reasoning models, while selected-head ablation improves refusal-related outcomes; these results concern refusal mediation in reasoning models but do not test the original single-direction intervention (rows r1–r19).
